title: Read in Daily Life: longer texts
lines: The longer version of Read in Daily Life gives you a practical text of about 90-160 words with three questions. The texts are the ones a student deals with every week: an email from a landlord, a campus announcement, a flyer for a workshop, instructions for a new device, a web page about library services, or a short thread of messages between two people.
## What is on the screen
- One text, laid out to look like its real form: an email with a subject line, a poster with headings, a web page with sections, or a message thread with names and times.
- Three multiple-choice questions, four options each.
- Question types: the purpose of the text, a detail, an inference, the meaning of a word or phrase in context, and what someone will probably do next.
## Timing
This task is part of the Reading module (about 30 minutes for all of Reading, in two stages). Aim for about 2 to 2.5 minutes per text: around 50 seconds to read, then about 30 seconds per question.
## What is being tested
- Following the organization of a practical text: headings, steps, conditions and exceptions.
- Locating information quickly and reading it exactly.
- Making a small inference: what is implied but not stated.
- Understanding a word's meaning in this context, which may differ from its most common meaning.
- Understanding a sequence of messages: who asked, who answered, and what was agreed.
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Use the layout. Read the subject line, title or headings first. In a thread, note who is writing and in what order.
- Step 2: Read the text once at a steady pace. Notice the purpose (often stated in the first two lines) and any change, request, condition or deadline.
- Step 3: Read each question and decide its type. Purpose and inference questions need the whole text; detail and vocabulary questions need one line.
- Step 4: For detail questions, find the exact place and compare carefully. For vocabulary questions, replace the word with each option and keep the one that keeps the meaning of the sentence.
- Step 5: For inference questions, choose the option that must be true from the text, not one that might be true.
- Step 6: For next-action questions, look at the end of the text: the last request, the next step or the agreement in a thread.
## Worked example 1
> Subject: Laundry room update
> Dear residents of Maple Hall,

> The two washing machines on the ground floor will be replaced next week. Work begins Monday morning and should be finished by Wednesday evening. During this time, please use the laundry room in Birch Hall, which is open 24 hours with your student card. The new machines will accept payment by card or through the campus app, so you will no longer need coins. If you still have credit on an old laundry card, bring it to the front desk before the end of the month to have the balance moved to your student account.
> Thank you for your patience,
> Sofia Reyes, Residence Office
> Question 1: What is the main purpose of the email?
> A. To explain how to use the campus app
> B. To inform residents about a temporary change and new equipment
> C. To ask residents to clean the laundry room
> D. To announce that Birch Hall will close next week

B covers the whole email: machines are out for a few days, there is a place to go meanwhile, and new machines are coming. A is a minor detail. C is not mentioned. D reverses the information: Birch Hall is the alternative and stays open.
> Question 2: The word "balance" in the email is closest in meaning to
> A. stability
> B. comparison
> C. remaining money
> D. payment method

In "have the balance moved to your student account", balance means the money left on the card, so C. A is the most common meaning of "balance" (keeping steady), which is a typical trap in vocabulary questions.
> Question 3: What should a resident with an old laundry card probably do?
> A. Throw the card away after Wednesday
> B. Use it in the Birch Hall machines
> C. Take it to the front desk soon
> D. Add coins to it at the new machines

C follows from the last instruction: bring it to the front desk before the end of the month. A ignores the money still on the card; B and D are not supported, and D also contradicts "no longer need coins".
## Worked example 2: a message thread
In a thread, track the conversation like a story: who asks, who offers, and what is finally agreed.
> Chen (9:02): Does anyone have a calculator I could borrow for Thursday's statistics exam? Mine stopped working.
> Amara (9:10): I have one, but I need it for my own exam on Thursday morning. It finishes at noon.
> Chen (9:12): That's perfect, mine isn't until 3. Could I pick it up from you at lunch?
> Amara (9:15): Sure. I'll be in the cafeteria by 12:30.
> Question: What will Amara probably do on Thursday?
> A. Take Chen's statistics exam with him
> B. Use the calculator and then give it to Chen
> C. Buy Chen a new calculator at lunch
> D. Lend the calculator to Chen before 9:00

B combines the final agreement: she uses it in the morning and hands it over at lunch. D gets the order wrong, and A and C invent actions. Wrong options in threads often give the right object to the wrong person or at the wrong time.
## Common traps
- The most common meaning of a word, when the context needs a less common one (balance, issue, figure, cover, note, run).
- An option that is true according to one line but not the main purpose.
- Possible but not stated: inference answers must be supported by the text.
- Reversed roles in threads: who asked and who offered.
- Conditions and exceptions: "students who registered before May 1", "except holidays", "unless it rains".
! Before you choose an inference answer, point to the line that supports it. If you cannot point, it is probably a trap.
## How to practise between mocks
- Read university web pages in English: housing, library, IT help, student services. They are exactly this style.
- Practise vocabulary in context: write down common words with a second meaning (a "figure" in a report, to "run" a club, to "cover" a shift).
- After reading an email or notice, summarize it in one sentence of your own words; this trains purpose questions.
- Time yourself: three questions in about two and a half minutes, then review each wrong option and name its trap type.
